Series::CalcAccessor::diff¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Related Accessor Methods¶

x.calc.diff is also an accessor with named methods for stochastic calculus: ito, strat, marcus, malliavin and skorokhod. They are documented on their own pages, linked under See Also. The call form on this page is unchanged.

Signatures¶

template<class Fn>
Series Series::CalcAccessor::diff(Fn&& fn) const

template<class Fn>
Series Series::CalcAccessor::diff(Fn&& fn, std::int64_t order) const

What It Computes¶

diff() differentiates a callable at the owning Series. It evaluates fn with a fresh differentiable copy of the receiver, follows the graph made by ordinary Series operations, and returns the requested derivative. It does not estimate a slope by perturbing input values, so there is no step-size option or finite-difference truncation error.

The default order is one. Order zero evaluates fn(x) and returns its value. For order greater than one, each reverse pass retains a differentiable graph for the next pass. An operation on the path must therefore support the requested derivative depth, not merely a first reverse rule.

This method is unrelated to root Series::diff(), which subtracts adjacent stored elements.

Full Derivative Geometry¶

Let fn(x) have shape Y and x have shape X. In the default mode, order n returns shape

Y + X + X + ... + X
    \_____ n copies _____/

Output axes come first. Every derivative axis block uses the receiver’s full shape, not a flattened public shape. For vector-to-vector first derivatives, this is the familiar Jacobian. For a scalar output at order two, it is the Hessian. Higher-rank input and output axes remain visible, allowing callers to contract or rearrange them without reconstructing indices from a flat matrix.

Elementwise Geometry¶

Set elementwise=true when every output lane depends only on its corresponding input lane and only the diagonal derivative is needed. The callback must return the receiver’s exact shape. The result keeps that shape at every order:

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.elementwise = true;
auto diagonal = x.calc(options).diff(fn, 4);

This costs one reverse pass per order rather than materializing all combinations of input lanes. Do not use it for coupled functions merely because input and output shapes happen to match; off-diagonal dependencies would be deliberately discarded.

Dependency Policy¶

With the default strict_dependency=false, a callback result that genuinely does not depend on the receiver contributes zeros. With strict_dependency=true, a disconnected path throws and names the derivative order at which dependency disappeared.

The higher-order engine separately tracks whether reverse results remain differentiable. If an operation supports first order but detaches its reverse result, a later order fails closed rather than being mistaken for zero.

Examples¶

Example 1. A product of transcendental functions needs no hand-written product or chain rule at the call site. The graph composes both rules through fourth order.

auto x = pluss::make_series(0.5);
auto fn = [](const pluss::Series& z) {
  return z.log().mul(z.asin());
};

std::cout << std::setprecision(10);
std::cout << "value=" << x.calc.diff(fn, 0).item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "first=" << x.calc.diff(fn, 1).item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "fourth=" << x.calc.diff(fn, 4).item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

value=-0.3629310151
first=0.2468201286
fourth=19.8335025

Example 2. The default first derivative of a vector-valued function is the full Jacobian. sin() is lane-local, so only the diagonal is nonzero.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 1.5});
auto jacobian = x.calc.diff(
    [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.sin(); });

std::cout << jacobian << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=9, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.87758256, 0, 0],
  [0, 0.54030231, 0],
  [0, 0, 0.070737202]]

Example 3. Elementwise mode extracts that diagonal directly and keeps the receiver shape. A fourth derivative of sine returns sine again.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.elementwise = true;

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 1.5});
auto sine = [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.sin(); };

std::cout << "first=" << x.calc(options).diff(sine) << "\n";
std::cout << "fourth=" << x.calc(options).diff(sine, 4) << "\n";

Output¶

first=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.87758256, 0.54030231, 0.070737202]
fourth=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.47942554, 0.84147098, 0.99749499]

Example 4. Elementwise differentiation is rank-polymorphic. For z^3, the second derivative is 6z lane by lane.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.elementwise = true;

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto result = x.calc(options).diff(
    [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.pow(3.0); }, 2);

std::cout << result << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[6, 12],
  [18, 24]]

Example 5. A detached constant returns zeros under the default policy.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.elementwise = true;

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 1.5});
auto constant = [](const pluss::Series& z) {
  return z.mul(0.0).add(7.0).detach();
};

std::cout << x.calc(options).diff(constant) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 6. Strict mode turns the same missing dependency into a diagnostic, which is useful when a detached path is more likely to be a model bug than an intentional constant.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.elementwise = true;
options.strict_dependency = true;

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 1.5});
auto constant = [](const pluss::Series& z) {
  return z.mul(0.0).add(7.0).detach();
};

try {
  (void)x.calc(options).diff(constant);
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::string message = error.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

Series.calc.diff: the function does not depend on x at derivative order 1

Receiver State And Platform¶

The receiver need not be a leaf and need not have tracking enabled. diff() creates its own leaf and leaves the receiver’s tracking flag and stored sensitivity unchanged. The derivative remains on the receiver’s platform; no CPU transfer is part of the calculus contract.

The callback should keep its result on that platform. Host extraction inside the callback breaks graph composition and prevents batched accelerator work.

Performance¶

Full higher-order derivative tensors grow as the product of all output lanes and one complete input lane set per order. That geometry is inherently large: a length-N vector-to-vector nth derivative has N^(n+1) entries. Prefer:

  • elementwise=true for genuinely lane-local functions;

  • grad for scalar objectives when only first order is needed;

  • hess for a scalar second derivative with an explicit contract;

  • contractions inside the callback when the full output geometry is not required.

Failure Modes¶

  • order must be non-negative.

  • The callback must return a defined Series.

  • Elementwise mode requires the callback output shape to equal the input shape.

  • Strict mode rejects a disconnected derivative path.

  • A higher-order request rejects reverse paths that are not themselves differentiable.

  • Shape growth and allocation limits still apply to full derivative tensors.
